newsitem.title: CHINA: California's Wilson stresses China trade over rights.
newsitem.headline: California's Wilson stresses China trade over rights.

text.p: California Governor Pete Wilson steered clear of the sensitive issue of human rights in China on Thursday, emphasising trade and saying political stability was a mutual goal of Beijing and Washington.

"We think that economic growth can also produce the kind of political stability that is clearly desired on both sides of the Pacific," Wilson told a news conference in Shanghai, speaking on the last day of a three-week swing through Asia.
"I think they (trade and human rights) are disparate concerns."

Wilson said the emphasis of his trade mission, which has also taken him to Hong Kong, Indonesia, Singapore, Thailand, the Philippines, and Taiwan, was the promotion of California's companies, exporters and investment opportunities.

California's exports to China grew 55 percent in the first nine months of 1996 to $1.47 billion, after falling 13.2 percent in 1995, U.S. figures show. Total U.S. exports to China fell 2.2 percent in the first nine months of 1996, the figures show.

China is currently California's 16th largest export market, with 60 percent of merchandise exports in key high-technology manufacturing industries including aircraft and aerospace, industrial machinery, computers and electronics.

Wilson, a 1996 Republican presidential hopeful until he quit the race in September, was in Shanghai on the eve of the release of what was expected to be a hard-hitting U.S. government report on Beijing's human rights situation.
The report says that by the end of 1996, there were no active dissidents left in China who had not been jailed or exiled, U.S. officials have said.
Nevertheless the Sino-U.S. relationship has warmed rapidly in recent months.
Beijing announced on Thursday U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright will visit in late February in a trip aimed at further improving ties.

On Thursday, U.S. trade offical Lee Sands began talks in Beijing to discuss China's delayed accession to the World Trade Organisation, long a source of cross-Pacific tension. Beijing has accused Washington of blocking its entry.
U.S. trade officials have also been in China this week for talks on renewing a textile accord and resolving a dispute over U.S. penalties on Chinese exports.
